$comment: THE CONTRACT BETWEEN THE EXPORT PIPELINE AND THE APP.
tools/avatar-export/export_anny_glb.py emits exactly these morph target
names. app/src/features/avatar3d/bodyModel.ts matches them by name to
decide which body axis each one drives.
Nothing at runtime connects those two facts. If a name here drifts from
what bodyModel's candidate lists recognise, applyShapeToObject finds no
morph targets, silently falls back to whole-mesh axis scaling, and the
avatar keeps responding to the sliders — by stretching geometry instead of
deforming a body. It looks like it works. That is the whole failure mode
the mesh upgrade exists to escape, and a typo here reintroduces it.
So this file is asserted from BOTH sides:
- Python: export_anny_glb.py --self-check validates it before exporting.
- TypeScript: humanBase/__tests__/morphContract.test.ts feeds every name
below through the REAL matcher and asserts it binds to the intended
axis in the intended mode. That test fails in CI if either side moves.
WHY PAIRS AND NOT ONE SLIDER PER AXIS.
A glTF morph target interpolates from the base mesh (influence 0) toward
the target (influence 1). A single bidirectional slider resting at 0.5
therefore requires the BASE MESH to be one extreme — the short, thin body —
so anything that renders before shape is applied, or at all-zero influences
(a failed shape pass, a frame before the effect runs, a tool opening the
GLB cold), shows that extreme rather than a neutral person.
With pairs the base mesh is neutral and all-zero influences ARE the rest
pose, so every one of those cases degrades to a normal body. It costs 8
morph targets instead of 4 — negligible against the 60 that
inspectHumanBase starts warning at, and against the 564 Anny ships.
baseMesh: neutral phenotype — all-zero influences must look like a person
naming$comment: Each name above was chosen to survive bodyModel's longest-match
classification, which is not as simple as it looks.
Matching is name-contains-candidate, so the candidate lists overlap:
'chestsmall' contains 'chest', 'overweight' contains 'weight'. The
classifier resolves that by taking the LONGEST matching candidate as the
most specific description of a name. Consequences worth knowing before
renaming anything here:
Short       -> negative 'short'. NOT 'HeightShort': that contains the
neutral candidate 'height', and while longest-match still
picks 'heightshort'... there is no such candidate, so it
would fall to neutral 'height' and read as a bidirectional
slider resting at 0.5.
Tall        -> positive 'tall'.
Thin        -> negative 'thin'.
Heavy       -> positive 'heavy'. NOT 'Overweight', which also works but
is longer for no gain.
ChestSmall  -> negative 'chestsmall' (10) beats neutral 'chest' (5).
ChestLarge  -> positive 'chestlarge' (10) beats neutral 'chest' (5).
HipNarrow   -> negative 'hipnarrow' (9) beats neutral 'hip' (3).
HipWide     -> positive 'hipwide' (7) beats neutral 'hip' (3).
If you need a different name, add its candidate to
MORPH_TARGET_NAME_CANDIDATES in bodyModel.ts rather than hoping the
substring happens to land — and let the TypeScript test confirm it.
annyPhenotype$comment: `annyPhenotype` names the Anny phenotype axis each pole is sampled from,
and `value` the position on it (Anny phenotypes are 0..1 with 0.5 neutral).
THESE ARE UNVERIFIED. Anny exposes semantic phenotypes documented as
including gender, age, height, weight and muscle plus local features; the
exact attribute names for bust and hip have not been read off a real
install. export_anny_glb.py resolves them through the model's own attribute
list and FAILS LOUDLY naming what it found if one is missing, rather than
silently exporting a mesh with two of the four axes flat.
